summary: This unit teaches you to get a client ready for any salon service: receive her, prepare a clean and safe station, carry out a consultation, analyse her hair and scalp, do the tests a service needs, and spot the conditions that stop or change a service. You will also learn to gown, protect and seat every kind of client correctly, and to keep accurate, private client records.

blocks.p: Every salon service starts before the first comb touches the hair. In this unit you learn the steps that come first: receiving the client, getting the station ready, finding out what she wants, checking that her hair and scalp are fit for the service, protecting her clothes and skin, and writing it all down. It is for COSMETOLOGY LEVEL 2 trainees, and you will use it in every other unit, from shampooing to colouring and relaxing.

Good preparation is what keeps a client safe. Most salon accidents and complaints can be traced back to something missed at this stage: a skin test not done, a sore scalp not seen, a relaxer put on hair that had a home colour, a cape fastened badly. So this unit is about **looking, asking, listening and recording** as much as it is about gowns and towels.

What this means in the salon

Greet her promptly and check her booking
Look after her belongings and her comfort while she waits
Prepare the work area
Clean and disinfect the station

Check electrical tools, the chair and the floor
Consult with the client
Use open and closed questions and listen actively
Ask about past services, allergies, health and lifestyle
Agree the service, the time and the cost

Note curl pattern, texture, density, length and condition
Test porosity and elasticity

Skin test, strand test and incompatibility test
Follow the manufacturer's instructions and record every result
Recognise contra-indications
Know which conditions stop a service and which only change it
Tell the client privately and tactfully, and refer her without diagnosing

Gown correctly for wet, dry and chemical services
Protect the skin, remove jewellery and seat the client safely
Adapt for children, older clients and clients with disabilities
Keep client records
Fill in the record card fully and clearly
Keep the client's information confidential and stored securely

flow: Agree the plan and record it

blocks.note: How you are assessed: theory papers (multiple-choice questions, short answers and essays) and practical tasks in the Centre's salon. In the practical tasks you work in a small group, taking turns as receptionist, stylist, client and observer. You carry out a consultation and a hair and scalp analysis, fill in a record card, prepare a station, gown a partner for a shampoo and for a chemical service, and show the steps of a skin test. No real chemical is used in these tasks.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.note: In practical work, photograph only the hair, scalp, hands, paperwork and work area. Never photograph a client's or model's face unless she agrees and the Centre allows it.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The way a client is received sets the tone for the whole visit. She should feel noticed, expected and looked after from the moment she comes through the door, even when the salon is busy.

flow: Tell the stylist she is here
Take her to the station and seat her

ul: Greet every client **promptly**, with a smile and eye contact. Use her name if you know it: 'Good morning, Mrs. Brown.'

If you are busy with another client, do not ignore the new arrival and do not shout across the salon. Look up, smile, greet her and tell her that someone will be with her shortly. Then carry on with your client.
Never leave a client in the middle of a service to start another one, and never leave a client alone with a chemical on her hair.
Keep your voice, your words and your appearance professional. Do not talk about other clients where anyone can hear.

blocks.p: Look at the appointment book or booking system as soon as she arrives. Confirm three things with her: her **name**, the **service** booked and the **stylist**. Check the time too. This catches mistakes early: the wrong day, the wrong service, or a chemical service booked without the skin test it needs. Mark her as arrived, so the stylist and the desk both know she is in the salon.

You will often be asked when a service will finish, or told to work out whether there is time for it. Add the hours first, then the minutes. If the minutes come to 60 or more, take 60 away and add one more hour.

head: Start
Service time
Working
Finish
rows: 1 hour 15 minutes
9:30 + 1 hour = 10:30; + 15 minutes
1 hour 30 minutes
2 hours 35 minutes
1:40 + 2 hours = 3:40; 40 + 35 = 75 minutes = 1 hour 15 minutes

ul: Offer to take her coat, umbrella, shopping or large bag, and put them in the place the salon provides: a locker, a cupboard or a coat stand.
Bags must not be left on the floor beside the chair, where people trip over them and hair, water and chemicals fall on them. They must not go on the station counter, among the tools and products.
Ask her to keep **valuables** (purse, phone, jewellery) with her. If the salon stores anything of value, it is labelled or recorded so that it goes back to the right person.
Tell her honestly how long the wait is likely to be. A client who knows it will be ten minutes is much calmer than one left to guess.
Offer her a seat, and water or another drink if the salon provides it. Reading material or the price list helps to pass the time.
Tell her stylist that she has arrived, and go back to the client with news if the wait grows.

blocks.note: Reception is the first thing a client sees, but in this unit it is only the first step. Receiving and directing clients, and booking and check-out, have their own units. Here, concentrate on getting the client from the door to the chair properly.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: The station must be ready **before** the client sits down. A client who watches you sweep up the last client's hair and hunt for a clean comb will not trust the rest of your work. A prepared station also stops germs passing from one client to the next, prevents accidents and keeps the service on time.

flow: Sweep; check the floor is dry
Set out fresh linen and single-use items
Set out only the products needed
Check electrical tools and the chair

ul: **Check the booking** first, so you know which tools, products and protective items the service needs.
**Wipe** the chair, armrests, counter and mirror with a disinfectant, mixed and used as its label says.
**Sweep** up all hair and make sure the floor is dry. Loose hair and wet patches are slip hazards.

Set out **clean, disinfected** combs, brushes and clips. A tool that has been used on another client, or has fallen on the floor, is not put on the station until it has been cleaned and disinfected, however new it is.
Set out a **fresh gown, towels and cape**. Single-use items, such as neck strips and disposable gloves, are new for every client.
Put out **only the products the service needs**, with their lids closed and their labels facing you. A cluttered counter leads to spills and to the wrong product being picked up.
Check that the dryer and other electrical tools work, and that plugs and cables are not cracked, frayed or loose. Keep cables out of walkways. Report a faulty tool and do not use it.
Adjust the chair, and check the basin and the water if a shampoo is part of the service.

blocks.note: Jamaica's power supply is 110 V (and 220 V for some heavy equipment) at 50 Hz. Check that a tool is made for the socket it is plugged into, keep electrical tools away from water, and dry your hands before you touch plugs and switches.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Word
What it means
In this unit
rows: Cleaning
Removing hair, dirt and product with detergent and water. It always comes first, because disinfectant cannot work through dirt.
Pull the hair out of a brush and wash it in warm, soapy water.
Disinfecting
Using a chemical that kills most harmful germs on clean tools and surfaces.
Soak clean combs fully in disinfectant for the contact time on the label; wipe the chair and counter.
Sterilising
Killing all germs and their spores, usually in an autoclave.
Used for some metal tools in other services.

ul: Tools must stay fully covered by the disinfectant for the whole **contact time** on the label. Mix it exactly as the label says and change it as often as the label says, or when it looks dirty.
Store disinfected tools in a clean, covered container, not loose in a drawer with used ones.
Use a fresh towel, gown and neck strip for every client. Used linen goes straight into a closed laundry bin.

blocks.h: Your hands and your own presentation

ul: **Wash your hands** with soap and water before you touch each new client and after you finish. Your hands are the commonest way that germs travel from one client to the next. Sanitiser is useful between washes, but it does not replace washing when hands are dirty.
Cover any cut on your hands with a waterproof dressing.
Wear a clean uniform or apron and closed, flat, non-slip shoes. Keep your nails short and clean and your own hair tidy and tied back if it is long.
Wear disposable **gloves** whenever you apply or mix a chemical product, and for any product whose label asks for them.

blocks.h: Know your products: the label and the safety data sheet

blocks.p: Read the label of every product before you use it. For chemical products (colour, relaxer, perm lotion, disinfectant), the manufacturer also supplies a **safety data sheet (SDS)**. It gives the product's hazards, how to handle and store it safely, what protective equipment to wear, and the first aid to give if it gets on the skin, in the eyes or is swallowed. Know where the salon keeps its SDS file.

blocks.note: Wipe up spills at once and put out a wet floor sign until the floor is dry. A slip on a wet salon floor is one of the commonest salon accidents.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: The consultation is a short, private conversation before the service. You find out what the client wants, learn the history of her hair, check for anything that could make the service unsafe, and agree a plan. It is done with the client seated, facing you or facing the mirror with you beside her, with her hair dry and in good light. Never skip it, even for a regular client: hair, health and home care change.

head: Skill
How you do it
rows: Active listening
Give her your full attention; do not look at your phone or around the salon
Let her finish before you speak
Repeat back what she has asked for in your own words: 'So you would like the length kept, and the ends curled under?'
Body language
Face her, at her eye level if you can
Keep eye contact, nod and smile
Keep your arms relaxed, not folded
Do not start brushing or handling her hair while she is still explaining
Plain words
Avoid salon jargon, or explain it
Check that she has understood: 'Does that sound right to you?'
Respect
Speak to the client herself, not only to the person with her
Do not criticise her hair, her last stylist or her choices

head: Type
What it is
Use it to
Examples
rows: Open question
Cannot be answered with one word. Often starts with what, how, when, why or 'tell me about'.
Get the client talking and learn what she really wants.
'What would you like done today?'
'How do you look after your hair at home?'
'Tell me what you liked about your last style.'
Closed question
Can be answered with 'yes', 'no' or one short fact.
Check or confirm a particular fact.
'Have you ever reacted to a hair colour?'
'Was your last relaxer in August?'
'Is this the length you mean?'

blocks.p: A good consultation starts with open questions and finishes with closed ones: open to explore, closed to confirm.

head: Ask about
Why it matters
rows: What she wants today, and the occasion
Sets the aim of the service and shows whether it can be done in one visit.
Chemical services she has had (relaxer, texturiser, colour, bleach, perm, henna, smoothing treatment), when, and whether done at home
Chemicals already on the hair can react with new products, or leave the hair too weak for another service. Home colours and 'colour restorers' may contain metallic salts.
Allergies, sensitive skin, and any reaction to a product in the past
Shows the risk of an allergic reaction. A past reaction to hair colour is a warning sign you must record and report.
Health: skin or scalp problems, medicines and creams, recent illness or surgery, pregnancy
May be a contra-indication, or mean the service must be changed. Some medicines affect the hair and scalp.
Home care: how often she washes, what she uses, heat styling, protective styles
Explains the condition you see, and shapes your product choice and aftercare advice.
Job, hobbies and daily routine
Lets you suggest a style she can manage and that suits her day: a nurse on shift, a swimmer and a bank teller need different things.
Time and budget
The service, and any follow-up visits, must be something she can keep up.

blocks.p: If she brings a picture, look at it **with** her. Ask what she likes about it: the colour, the length, the shape? Then say honestly what her own hair can and cannot do, given its type, length and condition, and what will suit her. Never promise an exact copy. A realistic promise that you keep is worth more than a big promise that you break.

At the end of the consultation, tell the client three things: **what** will be done, **how long** it will take and **how much** it will cost. Ask her to confirm. If the tests or the scalp check change the plan, explain the change and agree it again. Write the agreed plan on the record card.

blocks.note: Consent: for a chemical service, many salons ask the client to sign the record card to show that she agreed to the service after the consultation and tests. A client under 18 usually needs a parent's or guardian's consent for a chemical service; follow the salon's policy and the manufacturer's age limits (many colour products are not to be used on anyone under 16).
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: In the analysis you look at, feel and test the hair and scalp. What you find decides whether the service can go ahead, which products and how much heat to use, and how gently you must work. Do it on dry hair, in good light, before any water or product goes on. Wash your hands first.

head: Layer
What it is
Why it matters here
rows: Cuticle
The outer layer: overlapping, see-through scales that point towards the ends.
Its state decides the hair's **porosity** and shine. A flat cuticle is smooth; a raised or chipped cuticle feels rough.
Cortex
The middle layer and the bulk of the hair: fibres of the protein keratin, with the natural colour pigment (melanin).
Gives the hair its **strength, elasticity and colour**. Relaxers, perms and permanent colours do their work here.
Medulla
The soft centre. It may be missing in fine hair.
It makes little difference to salon services.

head: Feature
What it means
What you record
rows: Curl pattern
The shape the hair grows in.
Straight, wavy, curly or coily (from least to most curl).
Texture
The thickness of one single hair.
Fine, medium or coarse. Feel one hair between finger and thumb.
Density
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp.
Low (thin), medium or high (thick). Part the hair and see how much scalp shows.
Length
Measured from the scalp when the hair is gently stretched.
Coily hair shrinks, so do not judge its length by eye.
Chemical state
What has been done to the hair.
**Virgin hair**: never had a chemical service
Relaxed, texturised, coloured, lightened or permed
A mix, such as natural regrowth with relaxed ends
Condition
The health of the hair.
Shine, dryness, split ends, breakage, thinning at the hairline.

blocks.note: Texture and density are not the same. A client can have fine hair with high density (many thin hairs), or coarse hair with low density (few thick hairs). Record both.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: Regrowth and the line of demarcation

blocks.p: When relaxed or coloured hair grows, the new hair at the roots is untreated. The point where the new growth meets the previously treated hair is the **line of demarcation**. On relaxed hair it is a weak point: tightly curled, strong new growth pulls against straight, weaker relaxed hair, and the hair snaps there if it is handled roughly. Measure and record the regrowth (for example, 'about 4 cm'). The two parts need different care: a retouch product goes on the regrowth only, never over hair that is already relaxed, and the join must be combed and styled gently.

ul: **Porosity** is how easily the hair takes in liquids, and how well it holds on to moisture.
Take a small strand of dry hair, hold it by the ends, and slide the finger and thumb of your other hand along it **from the ends towards the scalp**.
Smooth: the cuticle is flat and tight; porosity is **low**. Products take longer to soak in.
A little roughness: **normal** porosity.

Very rough or bumpy: the cuticle is raised or damaged; porosity is **high**. The hair soaks up water and products fast, loses moisture just as fast, tangles easily and may take colour unevenly or too dark. Hair that has been lightened, over-relaxed or heat-damaged is usually very porous.
**Elasticity** is how far a hair stretches and returns without breaking. It shows the strength of the cortex.
Dampen a single hair, or a few hairs, with the water spray. Hold it firmly near the root with one hand and stretch it **gently** with the other. Do not tug.
Good elasticity: the hair stretches a fair way (wet hair can stretch by up to about half its length) and springs back.

Poor elasticity: the hair snaps after very little stretch, or it stretches a long way and stays stretched, feeling limp or gummy. The cortex is weak. This hair may not stand a chemical service; tell your supervisor, and expect to recommend conditioning treatments and a later date instead.

Use the tail of a comb to **part the hair in sections** and look closely at the skin, working over the whole head: hairline, behind the ears, crown and nape. Use a lamp or magnifying lamp if the light is poor.
Use the pads of your fingers, never your nails. Do not scratch or rub the scalp, especially before a chemical service.
Look for cuts, scratches, sores, redness, swelling, flaking, lumps, bald or thinning patches, lice and nits, and anything weeping or crusted.
Do not rely on what the client tells you alone, and do not leave the check until after the shampoo. Water, product and massage on an infected or broken scalp can spread the problem and cause pain.

blocks.p: The consultation, scalp check and gowning are the same for every client. What changes with tightly coiled hair is the handling. Coily hair tangles and shrinks easily and is often dry, so it needs more time and more moisture. Ask about her home care, any protective style (braids, weave, wig) she has just taken out, and the finish she wants: defined curls, a stretched style or a silk press. Before the shampoo, **detangle gently in sections** with your fingers or a wide-tooth comb, working from the ends up, with a little conditioner or oil if needed, and twist or clip each section to keep it apart. Look for build-up on the scalp and breakage at the hairline. Straight hair can usually be brushed through quickly before the shampoo, tangles less, and tends to look oily sooner at the roots.

Tests take the guesswork out of a service. Each one answers a different question. Always follow the **manufacturer's instructions** for the product you plan to use: they say which tests are needed, when, and how. Record every test and its result on the client's record card, with the date.

head: Test
The question it answers
When and how
rows: Skin test (patch test, allergy test)
Is the client **allergic** to the product?
Before colour and other products whose maker requires it. Usually at least 48 hours before the service, on the skin behind the ear or in the bend of the elbow.
Strand test
How will the **hair** take the product: what result, and how long to leave it?
Before or during a chemical service, on a small strand, often at the nape, or on a cutting of hair.
Incompatibility test
Is there something already on the hair, such as **metallic salts**, that will react badly with salon chemicals?
When the client has used a home colour, a colour restorer or an unknown product. A cutting of hair is placed in the test liquid.
Elasticity test
Is the hair **strong** enough for the service?
At the analysis, on a damp hair.
Porosity test
How quickly will the hair **take in** products?
At the analysis, on dry hair.

blocks.h: The skin test, step by step

flow: Explain the test to the client
Clean a small area of skin
Gloves on; prepare a little product
Let it dry; leave it uncovered
Tell her what to watch for
Check the result before the service

ul: The maker's leaflet gives the timing (usually **at least 48 hours** before the service), the place and the method. Some makers ask for a test before every colour, or again after a gap or a change of product.
Clean an area of skin about the size of a small coin behind the ear or at the inner elbow. Wearing gloves, apply a small amount of the product, prepared as the maker says.
Ask the client to leave the area alone: no washing, no covering, no scratching.
Tell her to rinse it off and contact the salon **at once** if she feels burning, itching or swelling.
Write the date, time, product, place and your name on the record card.
**Negative result**: the skin looks normal. The service may go ahead.

**Positive result**: any redness, swelling, itching, soreness, a rash or blisters. The service must **not** go ahead with that product. Do not shorten the timing or switch to another shade of the same product: the allergy is to the ingredients, not to the shade. Record it, tell your supervisor and advise the client to see a doctor.

blocks.note: An allergic rash caused by a product touching the skin is called **contact dermatitis**. In a severe allergy, the face, lips or throat can swell and breathing becomes difficult. That is a medical emergency: call 110 for an ambulance.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.p: A strand test shows what will happen on **this client's hair**. Before a colour, it shows the shade the hair will turn out and how long to leave the product. Before a relaxer or perm, it shows how quickly the hair is processing and whether it can take the product without breaking. If the strand breaks, feels gummy or gives the wrong result, change the plan or do not do the service.

Some home hair colours, 'colour restorers' and compound hennas contain **metallic salts**. These react with the hydrogen peroxide in salon colours, lighteners and perm neutralisers. The hair can get hot, change to an odd colour, or break. If the client's history makes you suspect such a product, a small cutting of her hair is placed in a mixture of hydrogen peroxide and ammonia, prepared as your instructor or the product maker directs, and watched for up to about 30 minutes. Bubbling, heat or a change in the colour of the hair is a **positive** result: salon chemicals must not be used on that hair until it has grown out and been cut off.

blocks.note: You may only carry out tests, and read their results, in the way your instructor and the manufacturer have shown you. If you are not sure what a result means, ask your supervisor before the service goes any further.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A **contra-indication** is a condition or situation that means a service should not be done, or must be changed. Some are found by asking, some by looking, and some by testing. You are not a doctor and you must not diagnose, but you must recognise the common signs and know what to do.

head: Condition
Cause
What you see
What you do
rows: Head lice (pediculosis capitis)
Small insects that live on the scalp
Itching
Lice moving near the scalp
**Nits** (eggs): tiny, oval, whitish specks glued firmly to the hair shaft, often behind the ears and at the nape
No service. Advise treatment from a pharmacy or doctor; rebook when clear.
Ringworm of the scalp (tinea capitis)
A fungus
Round, scaly patches, often with broken hairs or a bald spot; may be red at the edge
No service. Refer her to a doctor.
Impetigo
Bacteria
Weeping sores that dry to yellow, honey-coloured crusts
No service. Refer her to a doctor.
Folliculitis
An infection of the hair follicles, usually bacterial
Small red or white-headed bumps around the hairs; may be sore
No service over the area. Refer her to a doctor if it is widespread or sore.

blocks.p: After any infectious condition is found, put the towels and gown straight into the laundry for a hot wash, clean and disinfect every tool and surface you used, and wash your hands well. Tell your supervisor.

head: Condition
What you see
What you do
rows: Dandruff (pityriasis)
Small, dry, white flakes of skin shed from the scalp; may itch
Service can go ahead. Suggest a suitable shampoo. Heavy, greasy or inflamed scaling should be seen by a doctor.
Psoriasis
Red patches covered with thick, silvery scales, often at the hairline and behind the ears
Not contagious. Gentle services may go ahead if the skin is not broken or sore. No chemical service over open or bleeding patches; ask your supervisor.
Oily or dry scalp
A greasy shine, or tightness and fine flaking
Service can go ahead with suitable products.

blocks.h: Other reasons to stop or change a service

head: What you find
Why it matters
What you do
rows: Cuts, scratches, sores or sunburn on the scalp
Chemicals sting and burn broken skin and can pass through it into the body; infection can get in.
No chemical service until the skin has healed. Other services only if they can be done gently, away from the area.
A positive skin test, or a past reaction to the product
The client is allergic.
Do not use the product. Record it; advise her to see a doctor.
A positive incompatibility test
Metallic salts will react with salon chemicals.
No colour, lightener or perm on that hair.
Very poor elasticity, or breaking hair
The hair cannot stand another chemical.
No chemical service. Recommend treatments and review later.
A prescribed cream or medicine for the scalp or skin
The scalp is under treatment; a salon product may react with it or make the condition worse.
Check with your supervisor, and ask whether her doctor has said salon services are safe, before you go on.
Fever, or feeling unwell
She may be infectious, and she may faint or feel worse during a long service.
Advise her kindly to rebook for when she is well.
Recent surgery, a head or neck injury, pregnancy, a serious medical condition
The service, the position at the basin or the products may need to change.
Ask what her doctor has advised; tell your supervisor; adapt or postpone.

flow: Take her aside, or speak quietly
Say what you can see, not what you think it is
Explain why the service cannot go ahead today

ul: Be **private**: never announce a finding in front of other clients or staff.
Be **kind and matter-of-fact**. Lice and ringworm are common and can happen to anyone; do not let her feel dirty or blamed.
Do **not diagnose** and do not suggest medicines. Say: 'I can see a round, scaly patch here that I am not able to work over. I would like you to have a doctor look at it before we do your hair.'
Do not try to treat it yourself, cover it with product or 'work around it' to keep the booking.

blocks.note: If you find something during a practical task, stop and tell the assessor quietly. Do not carry on.
blocks.label: Safety

sections.title: Gowning, protecting and positioning the client

blocks.p: Gowning protects the client's clothes and skin from water, hair and chemicals. Done well, it also tells her that the salon is clean and careful. Wash your hands before you start.

blocks.h: First: jewellery, glasses and hair accessories

blocks.p: Ask the client to take off earrings, necklaces, hair clips and, where needed, glasses, and to put them in her own bag or pocket. Jewellery catches in combs and brushes, gets lost down the basin, is discoloured or damaged by chemicals, heats up under a dryer, and traps chemical against the skin.

head: Service
What you put on, in order
Points to watch
rows: Shampoo, wet set or blow-dry
Clean gown, fastened
Clean towel round the shoulders, crossed under the chin
Waterproof shampoo cape over the towel
After the shampoo: a fresh, dry towel or a cutting collar for the styling
The towel soaks up drips so that water cannot run down the neck onto her clothes.
Haircut on dry hair
Clean gown
Neck strip round the neck
Cutting cape or cutting collar
The neck strip stops cut hair slipping down inside the collar.
Chemical service (relaxer, colour, lightener, perm)
Clean gown
Neck strip
Towel
Waterproof, chemical-resistant cape; a second towel over it if the salon does so
Barrier cream on the hairline and ears, as the maker says
You wear gloves and an apron. Nothing she is wearing should be where a drip can reach it.

ul: The **neck strip** (or towel) sits between the client's skin and the cape. It keeps the cape, which is used on many clients, off her skin, and it stops hair, water and product getting inside the neckline.
Fasten gowns, strips and capes **firmly but not tightly**. You should be able to slip a finger between the neckband and the neck. Ask her if it is comfortable.
Tuck in collars and hoods, or ask her to remove a bulky jacket, so that her own clothes are fully under the gown.
Check the gowning again after the shampoo and after any move between the chair and the basin.

**Barrier cream** (or the protective base the maker supplies) is put on the skin around the hairline, over the tops of the ears and at the nape. It stops colour staining the skin and protects the skin from relaxer and other chemicals. Keep it off the hair itself, where it can block the product.
Ask about allergies before you put any cream on the skin.
**You** wear disposable gloves to mix, apply and rinse chemical products, and an apron to protect your clothes. Chemicals and frequent wet work cause dermatitis on stylists' hands.
At the **styling chair**: she sits right back in the seat, back against the chair back, both feet on the footrest or the floor, legs uncrossed, so that her head is level and your work is even.

**Adjust the chair height** so that you can work with a straight back and your elbows below shoulder height. Stand with your feet apart and your weight even. A good posture gives you better control of the tools and protects your back, neck and shoulders through a long day.

At a **back-wash basin**: she sits back in the chair with her neck resting in the padded dip of the basin edge; add a folded towel if she needs more cushioning. Her head tips back gently, not sharply.

If she cannot lean back comfortably (a stiff or injured neck, a back problem, dizziness), use a **front-wash** position, leaning forward over the basin with a towel to shield her face, or extra support.
Help her up and down, and let her sit up slowly after the basin.

head: Client
How you adapt
rows: A young child
A parent or guardian stays and agrees to the service
Booster seat, so that you work at a safe height; a small gown
Simple explanations; tools and products kept out of reach
Work gently and without delay: children tire and fidget
An older client
Give her time; speak clearly and face her
Ask about stiffness, dizziness, medicines and thin or fragile skin
Extra neck support or a front-wash; help in and out of the chair
Fasten the cape loosely; check the water temperature carefully
A client who uses a wheelchair
Greet her and speak to her directly
**Ask how she would like to be helped**; never lift or move her, or her chair, without asking
Clear a wide path; move the styling chair away if she prefers to stay in her own
Adapt the set-up: your own position, a portable or tilting basin, a tray
A client with a hearing or sight difficulty
Face her; speak clearly; write things down if it helps
Describe what you are about to do before you do it, and guide her to the chair if she asks

blocks.note: The purpose of all this preparation is simple: a client who is **safe, comfortable** and gets the **result she asked for**. If a step does not serve one of those three, ask your instructor why it is done.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: A record card, or a computer record, is the salon's memory. It lets any stylist give the client a safe, consistent service, and it protects both the client and the salon if something goes wrong.

ul: To show what was done before, with which products and timings, and how it turned out, so that a good result can be repeated and a poor one avoided.
To show which tests were done, when, and the results, so that a product that caused a reaction is never used on her again.
To carry warnings forward: allergies, medical notes, contra-indications found.
To show what was agreed, if there is a complaint or a claim later.
To let the salon contact her about bookings.

head: Part of the record
What to write
rows: Client details
Name, phone number and other contact details; for a client under 18, the parent or guardian.
Health and allergies
Only what matters to the service: allergies, skin or scalp conditions, relevant medicines, past reactions.
Analysis
Curl pattern, texture, density, length, chemical state, regrowth, porosity, elasticity, scalp condition.
Tests
Which test, the product, the date and time, the place on the body, the result, and who did it.
Service
The date, the service agreed and done, the products with their shade or strength, the timings, the stylist.
Outcome and advice
The result, any reaction or problem, the aftercare advice and products recommended.
Consent
The client's signature where the salon asks for it, usually before a chemical service.

ul: Write clearly, in ink, at the time, not from memory at the end of the day. Date and sign each entry.
Write **facts**, not opinions. 'Client reports scalp itched after last colour' is a fact. Remarks about her character, her money or her private life do not belong on a record card.
Read the card **before** each visit and update it **after** each visit.

blocks.p: **Confidentiality** means keeping a client's personal information private. During a consultation clients tell you about their health, their medicines, pregnancies, hair loss and other things they would not tell a stranger. They do so because they trust you.

ul: Record only what the service needs, and use it only for her service.
Do not discuss a client with other clients, with friends or on social media. Share information with a colleague or supervisor only when they need it to serve her safely.

Do not leave cards lying on the station or the desk where others can read them. Paper cards are kept in a **locked** drawer or cabinet; computer records are protected by a **password**, and the screen is not left open.
Do not give a client's details, or even say whether she is a client, to anyone who phones or asks.

blocks.note: Jamaica's data protection law requires businesses to keep people's personal information safe, to collect only what they need, and to use it only for the purpose it was given. A salon's client records are covered by it.
blocks.label: Jamaica

ul: I can greet a client promptly, check her booking and look after her belongings and comfort.
I can work out when a service will end from its start time and length.
I can prepare a clean, safe station with disinfected tools, fresh linen and only the products needed.
I can explain the difference between cleaning and disinfecting, and say when I must wash my hands.
I can say what a safety data sheet is for.
I can carry out a consultation with open and closed questions, active listening and good body language.
I can say why I ask about chemical history, allergies, health, home care and lifestyle.
I can tell the client what will be done, how long it will take and what it will cost before I start.
I can describe the cuticle, cortex and medulla.
I can record curl pattern, texture, density, length, chemical state and condition.
I can carry out and explain the porosity test and the elasticity test.
I can explain virgin hair, regrowth and the line of demarcation.
I can check a scalp in sections and say what I am looking for.
I can describe the skin test step by step and say what a positive result means.
I can say what a strand test and an incompatibility test show.
I can recognise head lice, ringworm, impetigo, folliculitis, psoriasis and dandruff, and say which stop a service.
I can tell a client about a contra-indication privately and tactfully, without diagnosing.
I can gown a client for a shampoo, a cut and a chemical service, and explain each item.
I can position a client safely at the chair and the basin, and adapt for a child, an older client and a wheelchair user.
I can fill in a client record card and keep it confidential.

blocks.note: In essay answers, give the reason for each step, not only the step. For example: 'I place a neck strip under the cape so that the cape does not touch her skin and hair cannot fall inside her collar.'
blocks.label: Tip

terms: The conversation before a service in which you find out what the client wants and whether the service is safe.
A question that needs more than a one-word answer; it gets the client talking.
A question that can be answered with 'yes', 'no' or one short fact; it confirms details.
Giving full attention and repeating back what the client said to check you understood.
The messages sent by posture, face, eyes and gestures.
Looking at, feeling and testing the hair and scalp before a service.
The outer layer of the hair: overlapping scales.
The middle layer of the hair; gives strength, elasticity and colour.
The soft centre of the hair; sometimes missing.
The thickness of a single hair: fine, medium or coarse.
How many hairs grow on an area of scalp.
How easily the hair takes in and holds moisture.
How far a hair stretches and returns without breaking.
Hair that has never had a chemical service.
Untreated hair that has grown since the last chemical service.
The point where regrowth meets previously treated hair; a weak point on relaxed hair.
A test on the skin, usually at least 48 hours before, to check for an allergy to a product.
A test on a small strand to see how the hair takes a product and how long to leave it.
A test for metallic salts or other chemicals on the hair that react with salon products.
Ingredients of some home colours and colour restorers that react with hydrogen peroxide.
A reaction is seen: the service must not go ahead.
No reaction is seen: the service may go ahead.
A rash caused by a product touching the skin; it may be an allergy or an irritation.
A condition that means a service should not be done, or must be changed.
Able to pass from one person to another.
The eggs of head lice, glued to the hair shaft.
Ringworm of the scalp: a contagious fungal infection.
A contagious bacterial infection with weeping sores and yellow crusts.
An infection of the hair follicles: small red or white bumps around the hairs.
A non-contagious condition with red patches and thick, silvery scales.
Small, dry, white flakes of skin shed from the scalp.
A single-use paper strip placed round the neck under the cape.
A waterproof, chemical-resistant cape worn for colour, relaxer and perm services.
Cream put on the skin round the hairline and ears to protect it from chemicals and stains.
A basin the client leans back into.
Shampooing with the client leaning forward over the basin.
The maker's sheet giving a product's hazards, safe handling, storage and first aid.
Killing most harmful germs on clean tools and surfaces with a chemical.
How long a tool must stay wet with disinfectant for it to work.
The client's record of details, analysis, tests, services, products and advice.
Keeping a client's personal information private.
The client's agreement to a service; for a minor, a parent's or guardian's agreement.

c1.title: A first visit in Half-Way-Tree
c1.text: Miss Tanisha Gordon, 27, a bank teller, comes to a salon in Half-Way-Tree for the first time at 10:50 a.m. on a busy Friday. She is booked with trainee Shaneka for a relaxer retouch and style, which the salon allows 2 hours 20 minutes for. She is carrying a laptop bag and two shopping bags. Shaneka is still finishing another client's blow-dry and needs about ten more minutes. During the consultation Tanisha mentions that she put a dark 'colour restorer' from a pharmacy on her hair at home three weeks ago.

c2.title: Regrowth and rough ends in Portmore
c2.text: Mrs. Claudette Bennett, 44, a nurse in Portmore, has relaxed hair with about 4 cm of tightly coiled new growth. She blow-dries and flat-irons her hair several times a week. Trainee Oneil slides his finger and thumb along a dry strand from the ends towards the scalp and it feels very rough and bumpy. A damp hair from the crown stretches a long way and does not spring back. Mrs. Bennett wants a relaxer retouch today and a lighter colour next week.

c3.title: A colour for Saturday's wedding
c3.text: Mrs. Hyacinth Morgan, 52, wants a permanent colour at a salon in May Pen before her niece's wedding on Saturday. The maker's leaflet says a skin test must be done at least 48 hours before every colour. She comes in on Wednesday at 3:00 p.m. and trainee Kadian does the test behind her ear. On Friday morning Mrs. Morgan phones to say that the spot has been itching since last night and is now red and slightly raised. She asks whether she can still have her colour, as the wedding is tomorrow.

c4.title: Two scalps on one afternoon in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: At a salon in Savanna-la-Mar, trainee Roxanne has two clients after lunch. Jevaughn Stewart, 9, has come with his grandmother for a trim; on the crown Roxanne finds a round, scaly patch about 3 cm across where the hairs have broken off short. Her next client, Miss Paulette Dixon, 38, has red patches with thick, silvery scales along her front hairline; the skin is not broken. Miss Dixon says her doctor diagnosed psoriasis years ago and she is booked for a shampoo and roller set.

c5.title: Getting ready for a relaxer at the training salon
c5.text: In the Centre's training salon in Mandeville, trainee Tiffany is preparing her partner, Abigail, as the client for a relaxer gowning task. No chemical will be applied. Tiffany has put a chemical cape straight onto Abigail's neck and fastened it tightly so that it will not slip. Abigail is still wearing drop earrings and a chain. On the station are a tail comb that Tiffany dropped on the floor a minute ago and picked up, and six product bottles left from the morning session.

questions.q: Shaneka sees Tanisha come in while she is in the middle of the blow-dry. What is the best thing for her to do?
o: Finish the blow-dry first, then go over and welcome her properly
Stop the blow-dry and seat Tanisha at the next station to begin
Look up, greet her with a smile and say she will be about ten minutes
Wave her towards the waiting area and carry on without speaking
questions.why: A client should be noticed and greeted at once and told honestly how long the wait is, but the client in the chair is not abandoned. Finishing first leaves the new client ignored; waving her away tells her nothing.

questions.q: If Tanisha's service starts at 11:00 a.m. and takes the full 2 hours 20 minutes, when will it end?
questions.why: Add the hours first: 11:00 + 2 hours = 1:00 p.m. Then add the 20 minutes: 1:20 p.m.

questions.q: What should be done with Tanisha's laptop bag and shopping bags?
o: Stand them all on the floor beside her chair so she can watch them
Put them on the station counter where the stylist can keep an eye on them
Store the shopping in the salon's safe place; she keeps the laptop bag with her
Leave them all behind the reception desk for her to collect afterwards
questions.why: Bulky belongings go in the place the salon provides, and valuables stay with the client. Bags on the floor are a trip hazard and get hair and chemical on them; the counter is for tools and products.

questions.q: Tanisha has used a pharmacy 'colour restorer' at home. Why does this matter before her relaxer retouch, and what should Shaneka do?
o: It may contain metallic salts; tell the supervisor and test the hair first
It will have washed out by now; go ahead with the retouch as booked
It makes the hair resistant; use a stronger relaxer on the regrowth
It can irritate the skin; do a skin test today and relax the hair after
questions.why: Some colour restorers contain metallic salts that react badly with salon chemicals. The history must be reported and the hair tested (an incompatibility test) before any chemical is used; a skin test checks for allergy, not for what is on the hair.

questions.q: What do Oneil's two tests tell him about Mrs. Bennett's hair?
o: Low porosity and poor elasticity: the hair resists moisture
High porosity and poor elasticity: the hair is damaged and weak
High porosity and good elasticity: the hair is dry but strong
Low porosity and good elasticity: the hair is in sound condition
questions.why: A rough, bumpy feel from ends to roots means a raised, damaged cuticle (high porosity). Hair that stretches a long way and does not return has a weak cortex (poor elasticity).

questions.q: Given these results, what should Oneil do about the relaxer retouch she wants today?
o: Go ahead, but put the relaxer on the ends first as they are the roughest
Go ahead, but leave the relaxer on for only half the maker's time
Go ahead, as the relaxer only touches the new growth, which is strong
Tell his supervisor before going further, as the hair may not stand it
questions.why: Weak, over-stretchy hair may break with another chemical. A trainee reports the test results and lets the supervisor decide; treatments and a later date are usually the safer plan. Relaxer is never put on ends that are already relaxed.

questions.q: Oneil measures the new growth and notes where it joins the relaxed hair. Why does that join need gentle handling?
o: The relaxer from her last visit is still active just below the regrowth
The regrowth is more porous there and soaks up too much product
The scalp under the regrowth is thinner and more easily scratched
The hair is weakest where the coiled regrowth meets the straight relaxed hair
questions.why: The line of demarcation, where strong, curly new growth meets weaker, relaxed hair, is a weak point that snaps under rough combing or tension.

questions.q: Which entry on Mrs. Bennett's record card is written the way a record should be?
o: 'Hair in a terrible state; she clearly does not look after it'
'4 cm regrowth; ends very porous; crown hair stretches, no return'
'Hair damaged; client works nights and seems short of money'
'Normal relaxed hair; retouch booked; all tests fine as usual'
questions.why: Records hold facts that the next stylist can use: measurements and test results. Opinions about the client and details of her private life do not belong on the card, and neither do vague or untrue entries.

questions.q: Was Wednesday at 3:00 p.m. early enough for a skin test before a Saturday colour, according to the leaflet?
o: No: the test must be done exactly 48 hours before the colour
No: a test for a Saturday colour must be done by Tuesday
Yes, but only if the colour is applied after 3:00 p.m. on Saturday
Yes: any time on Saturday is more than 48 hours after the test
questions.why: From Wednesday 3:00 p.m. to Friday 3:00 p.m. is 48 hours, so the whole of Saturday is beyond the minimum. 'At least 48 hours' is a minimum, not an exact time.

questions.q: What does the itchy, red, raised spot mean?
o: A negative result: some redness is normal where skin was cleaned
The test was not left on long enough and must be repeated
A positive result: she is reacting to the colour product
The product was too strong for a test and should be diluted
questions.why: Any redness, swelling, itching or soreness at the test site is a positive result. It shows an allergic reaction to the product.

questions.q: What should the salon tell Mrs. Morgan about her colour on Saturday?
o: It can be done if the colour is kept off the scalp and rinsed early
It can be done with a darker shade from the same colour range
It cannot be done; she should see a doctor, and the result is recorded
It can be done if she takes an allergy tablet before she comes
questions.why: After a positive skin test the product must not be used at all, however short the time or different the shade. She is advised to see a doctor, and the result goes on her record so that the product is never used on her.

questions.q: Mrs. Morgan's sister, also a client, asks Kadian at the desk why the colour was cancelled. What should Kadian say?
o: That her sister had a skin reaction, since family have a right to know
That the colour was out of stock, so that no private detail is given
That she should ask the stylist, who can explain the test result to her
That she cannot discuss another client's visit with anyone else
questions.why: A client's test results and health details are confidential, even from family. Kadian should decline politely; inventing a reason is dishonest, and passing her to someone else who would tell her is just as much a breach.

questions.q: What is the patch on Jevaughn's crown most likely to be, and what should Roxanne do?
o: Possibly ringworm: stop, and speak quietly to his grandmother about a doctor
Possibly psoriasis: carry on with the trim, working gently over the patch
Possibly dandruff: shampoo with a medicated product, then do the trim
Possibly ringworm: trim the rest of the head and keep the clippers off the patch
questions.why: A round, scaly patch with broken hairs suggests ringworm of the scalp, which is contagious. The service stops, the adult is told privately what Roxanne can see, and a doctor is suggested. Working round it still spreads the fungus on tools and hands.

questions.q: How should Roxanne word what she says to Jevaughn's grandmother?
o: 'He has ringworm, so he needs an antifungal cream from the pharmacy today.'
'It is nothing serious, but salon rules say I cannot cut his hair today.'
'He must have caught something at school; you should keep him home.'
'I can see a scaly patch that I cannot work over; a doctor should look at it.'
questions.why: Say what you can see and why you cannot continue, and refer to a doctor. A stylist does not diagnose or recommend medicines, does not play the problem down, and does not guess at where it came from.

questions.q: After Jevaughn leaves, what must Roxanne do before Miss Dixon sits down?
o: Shake out the gown, wipe the comb with a tissue and change the neck strip
Spray the chair with air freshener and put the tools in the UV cabinet
Launder the linen, clean and disinfect tools and surfaces, and wash her hands
Rinse the comb under hot water and put a clean towel over the chair back
questions.why: Fungus can be carried on linen, tools, surfaces and hands. Everything that touched the client is cleaned and then disinfected, linen is laundered, and hands are washed before the next client.

questions.q: Can Miss Dixon's shampoo and roller set go ahead?
o: No, because any scaly condition of the scalp is a reason to stop
Yes, but only after a skin test for the shampoo and setting lotion
Yes, gently, as psoriasis is not contagious and her skin is not broken
No, not until she brings a doctor's letter to say it is not catching
questions.why: Psoriasis is not passed from person to person. With unbroken skin, a gentle, non-chemical service can go ahead with the supervisor's agreement; avoid scratching the patches and keep heat moderate.

questions.q: What is wrong with the way Tiffany has put on the chemical cape?
o: There is no neck strip or towel under it, and it is too tight
It should go under the gown, so that the gown catches any drips
It should be left unfastened, so that it can be taken off quickly
A chemical cape is only for colour; a relaxer needs a cotton cape
questions.why: A neck strip and towel go between the skin and the cape, to keep the shared cape off her skin and stop product getting inside. Capes are fastened firmly but never tightly: a finger should slip under the neckband.

questions.q: Why should Abigail's drop earrings and chain come off before a chemical service?
o: They make the skin test less reliable if they are worn near the ear
They stop the barrier cream from sticking to the hairline and ears
They may set off a reaction between the relaxer and the cape fastener
They can catch in the comb, trap chemical on the skin and be damaged by it
questions.why: Jewellery catches in tools, is discoloured or damaged by chemicals, and holds chemical against the skin where it can burn. The client takes it off and keeps it in her own bag.

questions.q: What should Tiffany do about the tail comb and the six product bottles on the station?
o: Clean and disinfect the comb, and leave out only the products for this service
Wipe the comb on her apron, and line the bottles up with labels facing out
Use the comb, as the floor was swept, and push the bottles to one side
Rinse the comb at the basin, and leave the bottles in case they are needed
questions.why: A tool that has touched the floor is cleaned and disinfected before use. Only the products the service needs stay on the station, so that nothing is spilt or picked up by mistake.

questions.q: Mr. Cecil Wright, 79, is booked for a shampoo and trim. He walks with a stick and says his neck is stiff. Which preparation suits him best?
o: Allow extra time, help him to the chair and offer a front-wash or more neck support
Seat him quickly at the back-wash and tip his head well back to keep his face dry
Ask his daughter what he wants and explain the service to her instead
Leave out the shampoo and cut his hair dry, without telling him why
questions.why: An older client may need more time, help with moving and a basin position that does not strain his neck. He is asked directly what suits him, and the plan is agreed with him.
